numberItems.stem: According to the handbook, getting **6 hours of sleep or less** does what to your crash risk?
numberItems.explanation: Being sleep-deprived (6 hours of sleep or less) triples your risk. The 40% figure is for working more than 60 hours a week; 15% is the share of heavy-truck crashes involving fatigue (p. 2-29).

numberItems.stem: A driver regularly works **more than 60 hours a week**. By about how much does this raise crash risk?
numberItems.explanation: Working more than 60 hours a week increases your risk by 40% (p. 2-29).

numberItems.stem: At least what share of all heavy truck crashes involve fatigue?
numberItems.explanation: The handbook says at least 15 percent of all heavy truck accidents involve fatigue (p. 2-29).

numberItems.stem: You notice you are yawning, drifting and missing signs. What does the handbook say to do?
options: Stop and sleep for the night, or take a 15–20 minute nap
Keep driving but take a break every 100 miles or 2 hours
Drink coffee — caffeine keeps you alert for a few hours
numberItems.explanation: If you notice any signs of fatigue, stop driving and sleep for the night or take a 15–20 minute nap; caffeine is not a cure (pp. 2-29–2-30).

numberItems.stem: How much sleep do adults need to stay alert?
numberItems.explanation: Adults need 8–9 hours of sleep to maintain alertness. Six hours or less triples crash risk; less than 5 hours is what long-haul drivers averaged in one study (pp. 2-29–2-30).

numberItems.stem: On a long trip, how often does the handbook say to take a break?
options: Only once you start to feel sleepy
Once per shift, at the halfway point
numberItems.explanation: Take periodic breaks about every 100 miles or 2 hours during long trips (p. 2-30).

numberItems.stem: What does the handbook say about using caffeine to stay awake?
options: It helps for only a few hours and then wears off — don't rely on it
It prevents fatigue for a full shift if you drink enough
It works as well as a 15–20 minute nap
numberItems.explanation: Caffeine can raise awareness for a few hours but eventually wears off; do not rely on it to prevent fatigue (p. 2-30).

numberItems.stem: You are on a dark rural road using **low beams**. About how far ahead can you see?
numberItems.explanation: With low beams you can see about 250 feet ahead; high beams reach about 350–500 feet (p. 2-30).

numberItems.stem: About how far ahead can you see with **high beams**?
numberItems.explanation: High beams let you see about 350–500 feet; low beams only about 250 feet (p. 2-30).

numberItems.stem: Dirty headlights may give only about how much of the light they should?
numberItems.explanation: Dirty headlights may give only half the light they should (p. 2-31).

numberItems.stem: [CA] It's a hazy afternoon. You must turn on your headlights when you cannot clearly see a person or vehicle at what distance?
numberItems.explanation: California law requires headlights when visibility is not sufficient to clearly see a person or vehicle for 1,000 feet (CVC §§280, 24400; p. 2-31).

numberItems.stem: At night, you must dim your high beams when an **oncoming** vehicle is within:
numberItems.explanation: Dim your lights within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle (p. 2-31).

numberItems.stem: You are driving at night and closing on a vehicle **ahead of you in your lane**. Per the CDL handbook, dim your lights once you are within:
numberItems.explanation: The CDL handbook says dim when following another vehicle within 500 feet. The 300-ft figure comes from the California car handbook (p. 2-31).

numberItems.stem: If you must drive in fog, which lights should you use?
options: High beams so you can see farther
Low beams and fog lights, plus 4-way flashers — even in daytime
Parking lights only, to cut reflected glare
numberItems.explanation: In fog use low-beam headlights and fog lights, even in daytime, and turn on your 4-way flashers (p. 2-32).

numberItems.stem: During a winter check, how much tread must your **front** tires have in every major groove?
numberItems.explanation: Front tires need at least 4/32 inch in every major groove; 2/32 inch is the minimum for other tires (p. 2-32).

numberItems.stem: What is the minimum tread depth for tires **other than** the front tires?
options: 4/32 inch — the same as the front tires
There is no minimum for non-steering tires
numberItems.explanation: Other (non-front) tires need at least 2/32 inch of tread; front tires need 4/32 inch (p. 2-32).

numberItems.stem: In winter, the radiator shutters freeze shut or the winterfront is closed too tightly. What can happen?
options: The engine may overheat and stop
Carbon monoxide leaks into the cab
numberItems.explanation: If the shutters freeze shut or the winterfront is closed too much, the engine may overheat and stop (p. 2-33).

numberItems.stem: In very hot weather, how often should you inspect your tires?
options: Only when a tire looks low
numberItems.explanation: Inspect tires every 2 hours or every 100 miles when driving in very hot weather (p. 2-34).

numberItems.stem: On a hot day your tire pressure reads higher than normal. What should you do?
options: Let air out until the pressure is back to normal
Let air out only if the tire is too hot to touch
Leave the air in — the pressure will drop as the tire cools
numberItems.explanation: Air pressure rises with heat. Never let air out, or the pressure will be too low when the tire cools; if a tire is too hot to touch, stay stopped until it cools (p. 2-34).

numberItems.stem: You must add coolant to a system with no overflow tank. After the engine is off and cooled, how do you open the radiator cap?
options: Protect your hands, turn it slowly to the first stop, and step back while pressure escapes
Remove it quickly in one turn so the steam escapes fast
Open it any time the temperature gauge reads normal
numberItems.explanation: Turn the cap slowly to the first stop to release the pressure seal, and step back while the pressure escapes; a cap you can touch bare-handed is probably cool enough (p. 2-34).
